headline_fact: A microscopic process can produce a visible gas.
summary: Yeast can release carbon dioxide during alcohol fermentation. Follow what changes inside the cell and what we can observe outside it.
did_you_know: Different fermentation pathways produce different end products.
core_mechanics: Alcohol fermentation releases carbon dioxide and regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
why_it_matters: The pathway connects cellular chemistry with observable gas production.
learning_takeaways: Identify the organism and pathway before predicting the products.

share_text: A visible gas can reveal activity inside microscopic cells.

biology_lesson.question: How can a yeast cell produce a gas?
biology_lesson.learning_goal: Connect a cellular pathway with a visible outcome.

conditions: Alcohol fermentation; suitable substrate and viable cells.

big_idea.explanation: A sequence of chemical reactions changes molecules. One step releases carbon dioxide, which can leave the cell as gas.

key_players.name: Carbon dioxide
key_players.role: A gas released during the pathway.

diagram.title: From a cellular reaction to an observable gas
diagram.caption: A conceptual pathway map. It omits intermediate reactions and does not show quantities.
diagram.description: Follow nodes one to three. A molecule changes during alcohol fermentation, releasing carbon dioxide.
limitations: Not an anatomical drawing or a complete reaction scheme.

nodes.label: Pyruvate
nodes.detail: Starting molecule for this simplified view.

explanation_steps.title: Start with the pathway
explanation_steps.explanation: Glycolysis produces pyruvate. This is the starting point for our simplified explanation.

explanation_steps.title: Identify the gas-producing step
explanation_steps.explanation: During alcohol fermentation, a reaction removes a carbon-containing group and releases carbon dioxide.

explanation_steps.title: Understand why the pathway continues
explanation_steps.explanation: A later step regenerates NAD+, a carrier needed for glycolysis to continue.

worked_example.title: An observable fermentation
worked_example.situation: Consider yeast carrying out alcohol fermentation in a vessel.
reasoning_steps: Connect that product with gas leaving the vessel.
worked_example.interpretation: Gas alone does not identify every reaction occurring inside the vessel.

change_scenario.question: Does every fermentation process produce this gas?
change_scenario.changed_condition: Replace alcohol fermentation with lactic acid fermentation.
change_scenario.expected_effect: The same carbon dioxide outcome should not be assumed.
change_scenario.explanation: The pathways have different reactions and end products.
change_scenario.limitations: This compares pathway types; it does not predict all activity in a mixed microbial sample.

misconceptions.belief: Fermentation always means the same process.
misconceptions.explanation: The organism and pathway matter when predicting products.

evidence.explanation: The identified reaction connects the cellular pathway with a gas product.

scope_limits: This lesson concerns alcohol fermentation in yeast.
uncertainties: Actual activity depends on the organism and conditions; this map does not predict a production rate.

key_terms.definition: A connected sequence of chemical reactions.
An electron carrier used in cellular reactions.

deeper_detail.title: Why regeneration matters
deeper_detail.explanation: Regenerating NAD+ allows glycolysis to continue. This supports energy transfer without making the two pathways identical.

knowledge_checks.question: Which gas does this pathway release?
knowledge_checks.explanation: Return to the gas-producing step in the map.

knowledge_checks.question: Can we predict the same gas from every fermentation pathway?
knowledge_checks.explanation: Identify the pathway before predicting its products.

takeaways: Name the pathway before predicting an outcome.
Connect the visible effect with a specific reaction.
Keep the limits of a simplified map in mind.
